en: Hey, this is Carlos, CEO at Product School and your host on The Product Podcast. speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: But you made it work. People recognize the name. It's obviously not very common, but the product works, so people find a way to remember it. You started this journey over seven years ago, way before LLMs became mainstream. I only started hearing about you maybe two or three years ago, so I'm curious: how did you see the opportunity in LLMs and decide to pivot into that? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:03:21 As I said, we started pre-AI, and honestly I didn't imagine we would ever do anything with AI at all. But then ChatGPT came along. We saw large language models getting stronger and better, and we started wondering how to make sure AI wasn't just a feature we bolted on, but that we actually participated in this wave, which we realized would be the future. So we took a step back and looked at what we were doing, and what our competitors were doing. All of us, including ourselves, honestly, were just sprinkling some AI on top. Then we thought: to really make use of it, we need to be part of the value chain. Not people using AI for anything, but people building AI-powered applications and agents inside n8n. That's when we realized n8n fits in perfectly. What do these large language models actually need? They need a lot of data from different sources, whether it's Google Drive, your local files, Salesforce, or whatever. The model does something with that data, it transforms it, it makes a decision, and then it outputs the data again into a system or a file. We already had all of those pieces in place. The pieces in between used to be done externally, or in a very limited way through HTTP request nodes. By adding these AI capabilities front and center, we were able to create something really powerful: not just simple automations, but genuinely powerful agents. The Secret Sauce Behind n8n's Traction

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: By the way, I love being wrong about those things. "Oh my God, now it's over one hundred million." There are so many tools out there trying to do something similar, and you weren't the first mover. Platforms like Zapier and Make had more market share. But you came out of nowhere in the last two or three years and achieved incredible traction. In the early days, what helped you get that initial tailwind? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:06:18 From the very beginning, it was all about power and flexibility. That's what we felt was missing from a lot of the existing platforms. With many of them you could build something very fast, but if you actually wanted to bring it into production or scale it, the platform maxed out. So we decided to really focus on power and flexibility, and to make sure people don't outgrow our solution. The other thing was our focus on the community, very early on. We created a great platform, but we also made sure people had a great experience: they support each other, we support them, we provided great support, we ran online events, and now we do offline events too. We put builders at the center. It's about empowering people. One of our core company values is literally "we are builders." We are builders, our community are builders, our users are builders. Having that alignment across everything attracts the right people and creates real value. We grew nicely in the first years, but it really took off when we focused on AI. There were a lot of other platforms out there, but none of them had the deep, powerful AI capabilities we built. They all had some AI integrations, so you could call out to OpenAI or something similar. But from the very beginning we made sure it wasn't just calling an API somewhere. You actually build proper agents: memory, multiple models, different tools you can configure easily, scripts you can add. That power and flexibility wasn't available anywhere else. That's what people really craved. Combine that with our other advantages, like the ability to self-host. People really appreciate knowing where their data lives, knowing they can run it behind their firewall, and knowing they can scale it. We have a big focus on reliability, scalability, and auditability, so you can easily understand what's actually happening, even in complex flows. Why n8n Let Everyone Self-Host for Free
zh: 顺便说一句,我很喜欢在这些事情上猜错。「哦天哪,现在已突破 1 亿了。」外面有很多工具在尝试做类似的事情,而你们并不是第一个入场者。像 Zapier 和 Make 这样的平台有更大的市场份额。但你们在过去两三年里横空出世,取得了令人难以置信的吸引力。在早期,是什么帮助你们获得了最初的那股顺风? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:06:18 从最开始,一切都关乎强大与灵活。这就是我们觉得许多现有平台所缺失的东西。对其中很多平台来说,你可以非常快地搭建出一个东西,但如果你真的想把它投入生产或扩展规模,平台就到顶了。所以我们决定真正专注于强大与灵活,并确保人们不会成长到超出我们方案的地步。另一件事是我们对社区的专注,非常早期就开始了。我们打造了一个很棒的平台,但我们也确保人们有很棒的体验:他们互相支持,我们支持他们,我们提供了优质的支持,我们举办线上活动,现在我们也做线下活动了。我们把构建者放在中心位置。这关乎赋能人们。我们公司的核心价值观之一就是字面意义上的「我们是构建者」。我们是构建者,我们的社区是构建者,我们的用户是构建者。让这种一致性贯穿所有事情,吸引了合适的人并创造了真正的价值。头几年我们增长得不错,但真正起飞是在我们专注于 AI 之后。外面有很多其他平台,但没有一个拥有我们构建的那种深入、强大的 AI 能力。它们都有一些 AI 集成,所以你可以调用 OpenAI 或类似的服务。但从一开始我们就确保这不只是调用某个地方的 API。你实际上是在构建正经的智能体:记忆、多个模型、可以轻松配置的不同工具、可以添加的脚本。那种强大与灵活在其他任何地方都没有。那正是人们真正渴求的。再结合我们的其他优势,比如自托管的 ability。人们非常感激知道自己的数据在哪里,知道自己可以在防火墙后面运行它,并知道自己可以扩展它。我们非常注重可靠性、可扩展性和可审计性,所以即使在复杂的流程中,你也能轻松理解实际正在发生什么。为什么 n8n 让所有人免费自托管

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: I want to unpack some of the concepts you mentioned. You built a visual layer that makes it easier for people, what you call "AI builders," to create these agent workflows. I think that expanded the market, because this isn't just a technical audience anymore; technically, anyone can be a builder. You also mentioned something unique compared to other platforms: you let people self-host your product. What was the rationale behind that decision? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:09:07 The core incentive is simple. When I started, I wanted a few things. First, I wanted to make sure we could become the default tool. And if you want to become the default tool, you have to make sure a lot of people can access it, and access it for free. That's really a requirement. The other thing is that I saw a lot of open-source tools out there building amazing communities that made their success possible in the first place. So it was very clear: I wanted to make n8n available for free, and open source was one of the directions I could take. But I went down a slightly different path, because I saw that a lot of open-source companies later changed their license to something more restrictive, and the community got very angry. Less because of the license they chose, and more because the company suddenly changed the rules: "first you could do all of this," and then they took some rights away. That really upset people. I thought, I can't afford that. Building a successful community is very hard, and it's also very easy to lose. So I decided to be upfront from the very beginning. I wanted to make it available for free for everybody, but I also wanted to build a business, pay my own salary at some point, hire a lot of people, and provide value. I wanted to make sure the money actually goes back into the company, because we reinvest it into support, docs, the product, and great events. Only by doing that can we keep growing and build a successful company. So from the very beginning I chose a slightly different license, which we now call the "fair-code" license. You can do more or less the same things you can do with open source. The only limitation is that you cannot commercialize the code itself. You can use it commercially inside your company at any scale you want, but you cannot build a hosted version of n8n and charge other people for it. I think that's a fair ask, which is why it's called fair-code. We did that from the beginning. We thought hard about how to enable scale, build a great community, and build trust, because trust is really the center of a community. People can say a lot of things, and they can change their mind tomorrow. But if you're consistent from the very beginning, so people see that what you say is what you actually do, you build a very strong community. It was very important to show that from the start, and over the last seven or eight years, people can definitely see it. The Free Tier as an Enterprise Growth Engine
zh: 我想拆解一下你提到的一些概念。你们构建了一个可视化层,让你所称的「AI 构建者」更容易创建这些智能体工作流。我认为这扩大了市场,因为这不再只是技术受众了;严格来说,任何人都可以成为构建者。你还提到了与其他平台相比一个独特之处:你让人们自托管你的产品。这个决定背后的理由是什么? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:09:07 核心动机很简单。当我开始的时候,我想要几件事。第一,我想确保我们能成为默认工具。而如果你想成为默认工具,你必须确保很多人能够获取它,并且能免费获取。这真的是一个必要条件。另一件事是我看到很多开源工具建立了了不起的社区,正是社区让它们的成功成为可能。所以很明确:我想让 n8n 可以免费使用,开源是我可以走的方向之一。但我走了一条稍微不同的路,因为我看到很多开源公司后来把许可证改成了更严格的条款,社区变得非常愤怒。这较少是因为他们选的那个许可证本身,更多是因为公司突然改变了规则:「之前你可以做这一切」,然后他们夺走了一些权利。那真的让人们很恼火。我想,我承受不起那种事。建立一个成功的社区非常难,而失去它却非常容易。所以我决定从一开始就坦诚相告。我想让所有人都能免费使用它,但我也想建立一门生意,在某个时点给自己发薪水,雇很多人,并提供价值。我想确保这些钱真的回到公司,因为我们把它重新投入到支持、文档、产品和很棒的活动中。只有这样做,我们才能持续增长并建立一家成功的公司。所以从一开始我就选了一个稍微不同的许可证,我们现在称之为「fair-code」许可证。你能做的事情和开源差不多。唯一的限制是你不能把代码本身商业化。你可以在自己公司内部以任何规模商业使用它,但你不能构建一个 n8n 的托管版本并向其他人收费。我认为这是一个公平的要求,这就是它叫 fair-code 的原因。我们从一开始就这么做了。我们认真思考了如何实现规模化、建立伟大的社区、并建立信任,因为信任才是一个社区的真正核心。人们可以说很多话,而且明天就可能改主意。但如果你从一开始就保持一致,让人们看到你说的就是你实际做的,你就能建立一个非常强大的社区。从一开始就展示这一点非常重要,而在过去七八年里,人们确实能看得清清楚楚。免费版作为企业增长引擎

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: I just went to your website, and you have this big button showing your GitHub repo with almost 200,000 stars, right next to the sign-up. It's a unique approach: you pursue this open-source path with a self-hosting option, and still find a business model that lets you run a business while making the product widely accessible. I've seen that approach in other companies, but not in your specific space. We hosted the SVP of Product from a database company that just acquired dbt, and MongoDB is often the lead example. But I think you're the first mover in automation. And by the way, how do you define your industry? I've seen terms floating around: automation, orchestration, now "loop engineering." Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:12:42 We're more like the orchestration layer, so "orchestration platform" is how I'd define it. But back to the previous point: a lot of open-source products start as open source and are very proud of it, and at some point they start to hide it. The source code is still there, but they try to hide it more and more and push people down the paid path. We very deliberately say the opposite. We obviously prefer if people use our hosted solution and pay us, because that lets us reinvest their money. But if people use us for free, that's totally fine as well. They're just two different ways of using n8n. The free option is super important for us. It's how we got adoption in large organizations: Meta, Nvidia, Dell, Accenture, and in Germany, Vodafone, Deutsche Telekom, Mercedes. We got into all of those companies the same way: someone had a problem, started with our free version, and brought it into their enterprise organization. That's what people underestimate. They think short-term: "How do I make sure this person pays me tomorrow for my hosted offering?" instead of thinking long-term: making sure people have a great experience and get a lot of value out of the product. When they get a lot of value, at some point they become a paying customer. And even if they don't, most eventually will. Bring Your Own Key and Switching Models
zh: 我刚打开你们的网站,你们有一个大大的按钮,展示你们的 GitHub 仓库,有将近 20 万颗星,就在注册按钮旁边。这是一种独特的做法:你走这条开源路线并带自托管选项,却依然找到了一种商业模式,让你既能广泛开放产品,又能运营一门生意。我在别的公司见过这种做法,但没在你的这个具体领域见过。我们 hosting 过一家数据库公司的产品 SVP,那家公司刚收购了 dbt,而 MongoDB 常常是主打案例。但我觉得你是自动化领域的第一个这么做的。顺便问一句,你怎么定义你们所在的行业?我见过一些说法在流传:自动化、编排,现在还有「loop engineering」。 Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:12:42 我们更像是编排层,所以「编排平台」是我对它的定义。不过回到刚才那一点:很多开源产品以开源起家并为此自豪,但在某个时点他们开始隐藏它。源代码还在那里,但他们试图把它藏得越来越深,并把人们推向付费路径。我们非常刻意地说反话。我们显然更希望人们使用我们的托管方案并付费,因为那能让我们把他们的钱重新投入。但如果人们免费使用我们,那也完全没问题。这只是使用 n8n 的两种不同方式。免费选项对我们超级重要。它就是这样让我们进入大型组织的:Meta、Nvidia、Dell、Accenture,以及在德国的 Vodafone、Deutsche Telekom、Mercedes。我们进入所有这些公司的方式都一样:某个人遇到一个问题,从我们的免费版开始,然后把它带进了他们的企业组织。这正是人们低估的地方。他们想的是短期:「我怎么确保这个人明天就为我的托管服务付钱?」而不是长期思考:确保人们有很棒的体验并从产品中获得大量价值。当他们获得大量价值时,某个时点他们会成为付费客户。而且即便他们暂时不付费,大多数人最终会的。自带密钥与切换模型

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: Even if someone chooses the free option, I imagine they start connecting different LLMs, and I know you let people switch between them. Some are open source, some aren't. How do you enable that optionality and still let people pay once they reach a certain level of usage? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:14:25 What makes n8n different from most other tools is that people bring their own key. We have some functionality where you can get test credits, and we're working on a feature where you can use LLMs and pay through us. But up to this point, people bring their own key. They say, "I want to use an Anthropic model, or an OpenAI model, or Hugging Face," and they connect it. Depending on their use case and their budget, they decide for themselves which one to use. An important part of n8n's power is that you can switch later. It's theoretically a one-second switch: just delete one node and put in another. But you'll usually have to make some adjustments too, so we also have functionality where people can create evaluations inside n8n to test what a change does and how they need to adjust, for example, their prompts. This is much simpler than changing your model provider on other platforms, especially if you switch from, say, an OpenAI model to the same model hosted by Microsoft. That's a switch of a few seconds. Market Positioning and the "X Killed Y" Cycle
zh: 即便有人选择免费选项,我猜他们会开始连接不同的 LLM,而且我知道你们让人们可以在它们之间切换。有些是开源的,有些不是。你们如何提供这种可选性,同时又让人们在达到一定使用量后付费? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:14:25 n8n 与大多数其他工具的不同之处在于,人们自带密钥。我们有一些功能可以让你获得测试额度,而且我们正在开发一个功能,让你可以使用 LLM 并通过我们付费。但到目前为止,人们都是自带密钥。他们说:「我想用 Anthropic 模型,或 OpenAI 模型,或 Hugging Face」,然后把它连接上。根据自己的用例和预算,他们自己决定用哪一个。n8n 强大之处的一个重要部分是你可以之后切换。理论上那是一秒钟的切换:删掉一个节点,放入另一个。但你通常也得做一些调整,所以我们也有功能让人们在 n8n 里创建评估,来测试某个改动会带来什么、以及他们需要如何调整,比如他们的提示词。这比在其他平台上更换模型提供商简单得多,尤其是当你从,比如说,一个 OpenAI 模型切换到由微软托管的同一个模型时。那只是几秒钟的切换。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: Right now, some Chinese open-source models are apparently performing better than some US-based models. Having optionality is an advantage: you're not locked into any provider. And you see in the news that when Anthropic or OpenAI releases a new model, the headlines say "this company just killed ten other startups." So I'm curious about your market positioning, your moat, and your relationship with these different providers. Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:16:13 There's definitely a lot of "killing" going on. "X killed Y" gets a lot of clicks, so it happens literally daily that something kills something else. I'd probably not take it too seriously. Most of the "killed" startups are still doing very well; obviously not all of them, so there's something true there. But what makes us special is our focus on auditability, flexibility, stability, and security, and really giving people control. The way I see it: the LLM is the engine, and we're the car, the roads, and the whole system. We connect everything and build the connective tissue between all these different models, agents, and business systems, and turn it into an actual process you can use. We all need each other. We need the model providers, and the good thing is you can replace them. You have a lot of models and a lot of systems you connect to, and we bring it all together. That lets you build not just a nice demo, but reliable, secure systems where you can actually understand what's happening. If you build an automation with n8n, you know exactly how your data flows, which tools it uses, and that it's not going to do anything else. When something goes wrong, you see exactly what went wrong. That's why large organizations choose us for business-critical use cases: they can get real ROI and deploy in production, not just build a nice demo. Live Demo: Building an Agent by Describing It
zh: 现在,一些中国的开源模型显然表现得比一些美国模型更好。拥有可选性是一种优势:你不会被锁定在任何一家提供商上。而且你在新闻里会看到,当 Anthropic 或 OpenAI 发布一个新模型时,标题会写「这家公司刚刚干掉了另外十家初创公司」。所以我很好奇你们的市场定位、你们的护城河,以及你们与这些不同提供商的关系。 Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:16:13 肯定有很多「干掉」在上演。「X 干掉了 Y」能带来很多点击量,所以几乎每天都有什么东西干掉了别的东西。我大概不会太把它当回事。大多数被「干掉」的初创公司仍然做得很好;显然不是全部,所以那里也有一些真实的成分。但让我们与众不同的是我们对可审计性、灵活性、稳定性和安全性的专注,以及真正把控制权交给人们。在我看来是这样:LLM 是发动机,而我们是车、是道路、是整个系统。我们把一切连接起来,构建所有这些不同模型、智能体和业务系统之间的连接组织,并把它变成一个你真正可用的实际流程。我们互相需要。我们需要模型提供商,而好消息是你可以替换它们。你有很多模型和很多可以连接的系统,而我们把它们全部整合起来。这让你构建的不只是一个漂亮的演示,而是可靠、安全的系统,你能真正理解里面正在发生什么。如果你用 n8n 构建一个自动化,你确切地知道你的数据如何流动,它使用哪些工具,以及它不会去做任何别的事情。当出了问题时,你能确切看到哪里出了问题。这就是为什么大型组织选择我们用于业务关键型用例:他们能获得真实的 ROI 并部署到生产环境,而不只是搭一个漂亮的演示。现场演示:通过描述来构建智能体

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: I think we've talked about the product enough. Now it's time to show it. I love that you volunteered to share your screen and demo. I'd love to see the product in action. Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:18:03 In the past, people built workflows manually. But with things like Claude Code, people realized building can be much simpler, and we realized it too. We want to give people that same great experience inside n8n, and let literally anybody build. A lot of the feedback we received was that n8n was a more complex system focused on technical users, and the goal was always to lower the bar. Thanks to AI, we're finally able to empower everybody to build. What you see here is our newest assistant, which we released about a week and a half ago. You just describe what you want to do. We give you some examples: say you have a marketing or SEO use case, you define what it should build for you. I prepared something in advance because it takes a few minutes to build. Here I asked it to build a personal workflow agent that works with my emails and my calendar. It starts with a chat trigger so I can talk to it. I told it my email address and everything it should be able to do. I also made sure to include human-in-the-loop: certain actions I don't want the AI to just do by itself. For example, I don't want it to send an email in my name without me confirming it. So I told it to make sure certain steps can't happen unless I approve them first. It started building, confirmed it understood what was going on, and then asked a first question, about which model to use, since there are a lot of models out there. I said, for example, use Claude via OpenRouter. It asked a few other questions too, and you can see its reasoning here. Then it kept building. Normally you don't have to care about most of this, but more technical users who want to understand what's happening can open it up and see exactly what the AI is doing as it builds the workflow. It built for a while, and then said it was done. I also said, "Actually, I want to change the way you built this slightly," and it went back in and made changes. In the end, you can see one of the artifacts here: the workflow it built. Let me make it larger so you can see it better. It's quite easy to understand. You start with a chat node where the conversation begins; you input the data, and it flows into this agent. By default this agent uses Claude, but we also configured a fallback model, because even Anthropic isn't always 100% reliable. You can say, "If this model is currently unavailable, fall back to GPT via OpenRouter." Then you see all the different tools we defined: get recent emails, get emails, create a draft, and so on. And here you see the human-in-the-loop steps: it can send an email, but only after I approve it. We can see the configuration of each node. Here, before approval, it shows a message: "Send this email, please confirm." It gives you an overview of who it's going to, the subject, and the body, and before it actually does anything it always asks for confirmation. Same thing for sending a reply, or for creating calendar events.
zh: 我觉得产品我们聊得够多了。现在是时候展示它了。我很喜欢你主动提出要分享屏幕做演示。我很想看看产品实际运行起来是什么样。 Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:18:03 过去,人们手工构建工作流。但随着 Claude Code 这类东西的出现,人们意识到构建可以简单得多,我们也意识到了这一点。我们想在 n8n 里给人们同样的绝佳体验,并让字面意义上的任何人都能构建。我们收到的很多反馈是,n8n 是一个更复杂的系统,面向技术用户,而目标一直是降低门槛。多亏了 AI,我们终于能够赋能每个人去构建。你现在看到的是我们最新的助手,大约一周半前发布。你只需描述你想做什么。我们给你一些示例:假设你有一个营销或 SEO 用例,你定义它应该为你构建什么。我提前准备了一些东西,因为构建需要几分钟。在这里我让它构建一个个人工作流智能体,处理我的邮件和我的日历。它以一个聊天触发器开始,这样我就可以和它对话。我把我的邮箱地址以及它应该能做的所有事情告诉了它。我还特意加入了 human-in-the-loop:某些操作我不想让 AI 自己擅自执行。例如,我不想让它在没有我确认的情况下以我的名义发送邮件。所以我让它确保某些步骤必须先经我批准才能发生。它开始构建,确认它理解了要做什么,然后问了第一个问题,关于用哪个模型,因为外面有很多模型。比如我说,用 OpenRouter 上的 Claude。它还问了几个其他问题,你可以在这里看到它的推理过程。然后它继续构建。通常你不用关心其中大部分内容,但想了解发生了什么的技术用户可以打开它,确切地看到 AI 在构建工作流时正在做什么。它构建了一会儿,然后说完成了。我还说:「其实,我想稍微改变一下你构建它的方式」,于是它又返回去做了修改。最后,你可以在这里看到其中一个产物:它构建的工作流。让我把它放大,这样你能看得更清楚。它相当容易理解。你从一个聊天节点开始,对话在那里开始;你输入数据,数据流入这个智能体。默认情况下这个智能体使用 Claude,但我们还配置了一个备用模型,因为即便是 Anthropic 也不是 100% 可靠的。你可以说:「如果这个模型当前不可用,就回退到 OpenRouter 上的 GPT。」然后你会看到我们定义的所有不同工具:获取最近的邮件、获取邮件、创建草稿,等等。而在这里你可以看到 human-in-the-loop 的步骤:它可以发送邮件,但只能在我批准之后。我们可以看到每个节点的配置。这里,在批准之前,它会显示一条消息:「发送这封邮件,请确认。」它会给你一个概览:发给谁、主题和正文,而在它实际执行任何操作之前,它总是先请求确认。发送回复也一样,创建日历事件也一样。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: In this case I see two different types of workflows: ones that can be fully automated, and ones that require human approval before they execute. Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:22:12 Exactly. It can run in the background: "Every time a new lead is created, create something in Salesforce for me," and it just does it automatically. Or you can have an internal chat system like this one, where I created a personal assistant for myself that works through chat. You can test it here, or use it via Slack or Telegram. Or you can expose it to your users. For example, a large online travel agency automated a lot of its support through an AI assistant built in n8n: 75% of customer requests go through that agent, where people change hotel rooms, change bookings, ask questions, and so on. The nice thing about that example is that people are actually happier with the AI customer representative than with a human one. That's amazing, because it shows AI isn't just about lowering cost; it can provide real value for users. So you can build anything from fully automated to "everything needs approval."
zh: 在这个例子里我看到两种不同类型的工作流:一种可以完全自动化,另一种在执行前需要人工批准。 Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:22:12 没错。它可以在后台运行:「每次创建一个新销售线索时,帮我在 Salesforce 里创建一个东西」,然后它就自动做了。或者你可以有一个像这样的内部聊天系统,我为自己创建了一个个人助理,通过聊天来工作。你可以在这里测试它,或者通过 Slack 或 Telegram 使用它。或者你可以把它暴露给你的用户。例如,一家大型在线旅游代理商通过一个用 n8n 构建的 AI 助手自动化了它的大部分客服:75% 的客户请求通过那个智能体处理,人们在那里换酒店房间、改预订、提问题,等等。那个例子的妙处在于,人们对这个 AI 客服代表的满意度实际上比对人类客服更高。这太了不起了,因为它表明 AI 不只是关于降低成本;它能为用户提供真实价值。所以你可以构建任何东西,从完全自动化到「一切都需要批准」。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: Got it. And just to clarify: this visual graph was created automatically based on the configuration you did before, right? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:23:39 Exactly, automatically. Normally you sometimes have to select which credentials to use. For example, for Claude you can use built-in credits, or use your own API key. You can do this with literally any tool: "This is connected to my Gmail account," and so on. So it builds automatically, and then you can go through and understand what was built. The problem with writing code is that you might have 10,000 lines you hope are right, but actually reading and understanding them is almost impossible; it can take more time to understand the code than to write it. Here it's simple. You have a chat node, you get a message, the data flows through, and here's the AI agent. You can see the system message that tells it "I'm an assistant, I have these tools, I have these rules," it gets the chat message, and it has access to these tools. You can easily add more tools, even code tools, actions in different apps. Anything your heart is asking for. 500+ Integrations, and Connecting to Anything
zh: 明白了。顺便确认一下:这个可视化图是根据你之前的配置自动生成的,对吧? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:23:39 没错,自动生成的。通常有时你得选择使用哪个凭证。例如,对于 Claude,你可以使用内置额度,或者使用你自己的 API 密钥。你对任何工具都可以这样做:「这个连接到了我的 Gmail 账户」,等等。所以它自动构建,然后你可以逐一查看,理解构建了什么。写代码的问题在于你可能有 10,000 行你希望是对的代码,但真正去阅读并理解它们几乎是不可能的;理解代码可能比写代码花的时间还多。在这里则很简单。你有一个聊天节点,收到一条消息,数据流经其中,而这里是 AI 智能体。你可以看到系统消息,它告诉它「我是一个助手,我有这些工具,我有这些规则」,它收到聊天消息,并且可以访问这些工具。你可以轻松添加更多工具,甚至是代码工具、不同应用里的操作。任何你心之所想的东西。500+ 集成,以及连接任何东西

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: A question about those tools. I saw on your website you have over 500 integrations. How do you handle that? Do you set each one up one-to-one, or is there a more automatic way to create integrations? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:25:20 There are multiple levels. There are built-in integrations that we create and maintain ourselves, the most important ones, like anything Google, or Salesforce. Then there are community integrations: the community builds them, we check them and make sure they're secure, and people can access them on the cloud solution or install them. There are actually a lot more than 500 out there. And even if there's no integration built by us or the community, you can still connect manually via an HTTP request node: make a GET or POST request to an endpoint. You can even ask the AI to configure the nodes for you. In the end, you should be able to connect to literally any API-based system.
zh: 关于那些工具的一个问题。我在你们网站上看到你们有超过 500 个集成。你们是怎么处理的?你们是逐个一对一地搭建,还是有更自动化的方式来创建集成? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:25:20 有多个层级。有内置集成,那是我们自己创建和维护的,是最重要的那些,比如所有 Google 系的东西,或 Salesforce。然后有社区集成:由社区构建,我们会检查并确保它们是安全的,人们可以在云端方案上访问它们或自行安装。实际上外面远不止 500 个。而且即便没有我们或社区构建的集成,你仍然可以通过一个 HTTP 请求节点手动连接:向一个端点发起 GET 或 POST 请求。你甚至可以让 AI 替你配置节点。归根结底,你应该能够连接到字面意义上任何基于 API 的系统。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: I remember the first time I set up my own agent. It was quite an ordeal, and I'm relatively technical, but there was no visual layer. Here I imagine you can drag and drop and set it up, and you don't need to buy a MacBook or a Mac mini to run it, right? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:26:29 Right, it runs entirely in the cloud, and you can test it easily. Let's say you tell it, "Send an email to James saying hello." I can literally watch the data flow through. The message is received, the agent starts, it adds data to memory, it calls the model, it figures out what to do next, and then it calls one of the tools. In this case it says, "Send out this email. Do you want to review it before I send it?" Because we set up human-in-the-loop, it stops and waits until I say to send it. I can say send or cancel. If something went wrong, you'd see the node marked in red and you could debug it easily. You can go in and see the logs, look at the inputs, see what was sent to the model, how it called a tool, and how it asked for approval. You can go through everything that happened and debug it, for literally any execution. Training Agents, Templates, and the Blank-Slate Problem
zh: 我记得我第一次搭建自己的智能体时。那真是一场煎熬,而我算是比较懂技术的了,但当时没有可视化层。在这里我猜你可以拖拖放放、完成设置,而且你不需要买一台 MacBook 或 Mac mini 来运行它,对吧? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:26:29 对,它完全在云端运行,你可以轻松测试它。假设你告诉它:「给 James 发一封邮件说你好。」我可以字面意义上看着数据流经整个流程。消息被接收,智能体启动,它把数据加入记忆,它调用模型,它弄清楚下一步做什么,然后它调用其中一个工具。在这个例子里它说:「把这封邮件发出去。你想在我发送之前审阅一下吗?」因为我们设置了 human-in-the-loop,它会停下来等待,直到我说发送。我可以说发送或取消。如果哪里出了问题,你会看到节点被标红,你可以轻松调试。你可以进去看日志,查看输入,看发送给模型的内容,看它如何调用工具,以及它如何请求批准。你可以逐步检查发生的一切并进行调试,对任何一次执行都是如此。训练智能体、模板,与白纸问题

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: Loops are hot right now: this concept of training your own agents, setting a goal, and having them improve. How do you think about that, and how can people train their own agents as they run these workflows? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:28:07 There's a loop happening already: you call the agent, it calls a tool, it goes back to the model, it calls another tool, it responds to the user, and it can go back again. You can also make it literally loop, telling it to talk to itself just by adding a connection here. It's very powerful; you can build very complex systems. Something happens here, it does something with the output, sends it to another agent, and that becomes an input again. People can build really complex use cases. Let me also show our website. Here are templates: over 10,000 templates created by our community. You can search "sales," or "Google Sheets," and see nice examples, like how to create TikTok videos. You click on one and see the actual automation that was built. You can explore exactly what's happening and how it was set up, and then just say "I want to use it," copy it, and paste it into a new workflow. The whole thing is right there. Now I can configure it with my own settings. In this case it has an OpenAI model, so I can use my own credentials or... Oh, sorry, I forgot the...
zh: Loop 现在很火:这个训练你自己的智能体、设定一个目标、然后让它们不断改进的概念。你是怎么看待这件事的,人们在运行这些工作流时如何训练自己的智能体? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:28:07 已经有一个 loop 在发生了:你调用智能体,它调用一个工具,它回到模型,它再调用另一个工具,它响应用户,并且它可以再次回去。你也可以让它真的循环起来,只需在这里加一条连接,让它和自己对话。这非常强大;你可以构建非常复杂的系统。这里发生了某件事,它对输出做一些处理,把它发送给另一个智能体,而那又再次成为输入。人们可以构建非常复杂的用例。让我也展示一下我们的网站。这里是模板:超过 10,000 个由我们社区创建的模板。你可以搜索「销售」或「Google Sheets」,看到不错的示例,比如如何创建 TikTok 视频。你点开一个,看到实际构建出来的自动化。你可以确切地探索正在发生什么以及它是如何设置的,然后只要说「我想用它」,复制它,粘贴到一个新工作流里。整个东西就在那里。现在我可以用自己的设置来配置它。在这个例子里它有一个 OpenAI 模型,所以我可以使用自己的凭证或者……哦,抱歉,我忘了那个……

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: I get it. This is a very important problem: starting with a blank slate is sometimes hard. Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:29:56 Exactly.
zh: 我懂了。这是一个非常重要的问题:从一张白纸开始有时很难。 Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:29:56 正是如此。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: So having a recipe that lets you validate what you need, while still being able to edit it based on your own tool stack and use case. Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:30:07 Exactly. And to finish the earlier example: I had the assistant build this workflow, but I can also extend it. I can say, "That's great, but now add a calendar tool where I want to book my one-on-ones with a consistent format, 30 minutes, and so on." I send that to the agent, and I can watch how it works. It goes off, does some thinking, and starts extending the existing workflow. So you can start simple. You don't have to build the whole solution from the beginning; you can do it iteratively. Start with the most basic version, then add other things over time. Now it's working, reasoning about what it should do. It'll take a few minutes. It figures out the different nodes it needs, checks whether credentials already exist, and says, "I need Google Contacts credentials. I already have an existing one," so it can connect to Google. In less than a minute it's done, and you can see it extended the existing workflow. That's the amazing thing: literally everybody can do that. You just have to know what you want to build. If you know what you want, you describe it, and it goes out and does it for you. Then you test it yourself, confirm it works the right way, and deploy it in production for daily use. The Multiplayer Bottleneck
zh: 所以,拥有一个让你能验证自己所需的东西的配方,同时还能根据自己的工具栈和用例对它进行编辑。 Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:30:07 正是如此。再补完前面那个例子:我让助手构建了这个工作流,但我还可以扩展它。我可以说:「很棒,但现在加一个日历工具,我想用它以固定的格式预约我的一对一,30 分钟,等等。」我把它发给智能体,我可以看着它工作。它跑开,做一些思考,然后开始扩展现有的工作流。所以你可以从简单开始。你不必从一开始就构建整个解决方案;你可以迭代地做。从最基础的版本开始,然后随着时间推移添加别的东西。现在它正在工作,推理它应该做什么。它会花几分钟。它弄清楚它需要哪些不同的节点,检查凭证是否已存在,然后说:「我需要 Google Contacts 的凭证。我已经有一个现成的了」,这样它就能连接到 Google。不到一分钟它就完成了,你可以看到它扩展现有的工作流。这就是了不起的地方:字面意义上的每个人都能做到。你只需要知道你想构建什么。如果你知道自己想要什么,你就描述它,然后它跑出去帮你做到。接着你自己测试它,确认它以正确的方式工作,然后把它部署到生产环境供日常使用。多人协作瓶颈

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: I want to ask about the main bottleneck I see with these assistants. People can now create their own second brains or AI staff, and that works well for their own productivity. But the multiplayer bottleneck is real. How do you create a shared environment where people benefit from each other's work and collaborate, instead of everyone building their own version of their own assistant? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:32:36 We're releasing something shortly, if it isn't out already, where instead of connecting your own credentials, you can assign credentials dynamically. So if I interact with it, it uses my credentials and accesses my Gmail and my calendar. If you chat with it, you give it access to your calendar, and it works for you. That's very important. Instead of 10,000 people in an organization each building something separately, you can have literally anybody deploy one thing, and the whole organization gets access to the same thing.
zh: 我想问问我在这些助手身上看到的主要瓶颈。人们现在可以创建自己的第二大脑或 AI 员工,这对他们自己的生产力效果很好。但多人协作瓶颈是真实存在的。你如何创建一个共享环境,让人们从彼此的工作中受益并协作,而不是每个人都构建自己那个版本的自己的助手? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:32:36 我们即将发布一个东西,如果它还没上线的话,它让你可以动态分配凭证,而不是连接你自己的凭证。所以如果我与它交互,它使用我的凭证,访问我的 Gmail 和我的日历。如果你和它聊天,你就给它你的日历权限,它就为你工作。这非常重要。与其让一个组织里的 10,000 个人各自构建自己的东西,你可以让字面意义上的任何人部署一个东西,然后整个组织都能访问同一个东西。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: Because ultimately we become super-agent managers, right? You have all these different agents doing different things. Sometimes they're yours, sometimes your teammates'. So what becomes the control panel, the surface for a product leader to understand what's going on and make modifications? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:33:45 I agree it's so important. By the way, you may have seen it go by fast: it's not just building the workflow, it's already testing it for you, so you can be sure that when it builds something, it's already in a working state. Getting Enterprises to Trust AI in Production
zh: 因为归根结底我们会成为超级智能体管理者,对吧?你有所有这些不同的智能体做着不同的事情。有时它们是你的,有时是你队友的。那么,什么会成为控制面板,成为产品负责人理解正在发生什么并进行修改的界面? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:33:45 我同意这一点非常重要。顺便说一下,你可能看到它一闪而过:它不只是构建工作流,它还已经在替你测试了,所以你可以确信,当它构建出某个东西时,它已经处于可运行的状态。让企业在生产环境信任 AI

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: Really cool. The other thing that's becoming challenging, especially for large organizations, is deployment. These demos work well when you have full control over the tools you're connecting. But as more people join, you have more controls and checks. For large enterprises already using n8n, how did you get over the procurement and guardrail problems so they trust your solution? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:34:32 Like we talked about, stability matters: people know where it's running, and they can often use their own local models to deploy. The other piece is that when you build with AI, it can go rogue easily. It deletes state it shouldn't, or sends emails it shouldn't. But because we make it simple, this agent can only do the specific things you've defined. It can't go rogue. You've specified exactly what it can do, including which things require human approval. That means before something goes into production, someone else can easily review it. And they're not reviewing 10,000 lines of code; they're reviewing a workflow they can easily understand and step through, so they know exactly what it will do. That makes it much easier for enterprises to trust it and release it in production faster than with other systems. Bottom-Up, Top-Down, and Partners
zh: 非常酷。另一件变得有挑战性的事情,尤其是对大型组织而言,是部署。当你对所连接的工具拥有完全控制权时,这些演示运行得很好。但随着更多人加入,你会有更多的控制和检查。对于已经在使用 n8n 的大型企业,你们是如何跨过采购和护栏问题的,让他们信任你们的方案? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:34:32 就像我们聊过的,稳定性很重要:人们知道它运行在哪里,而且他们通常可以使用自己的本地模型来部署。另一块是,当你用 AI 构建时,它很容易失控。它会删掉不该删的状态,或者发送不该发的邮件。但因为我们把事情做得简单,这个智能体只能做你定义过的那些特定事情。它不会失控。你已经确切指定了它能做什么,包括哪些事情需要人工批准。这意味着在某个东西进入生产环境之前,其他人可以轻松地审查它。而且他们审查的不是 10,000 行代码;他们审查的是一个他们能轻松理解并逐步走过的工作流,所以他们确切知道它会做什么。这使得企业更容易信任它,并比使用其他系统更快地把它发布到生产环境。自下而上、自上而下,与合作伙伴

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: This is a common challenge for companies that started in the SMB or direct-to-consumer segment, people building something and bringing it into enterprises. Beyond proving you have the right security checks, what does the go-to-market motion look like? Because product-led growth can only take you so far. Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:35:56 We got into most organizations via bottom-up growth, but interestingly, not only bottom-up. We also get in top-down, where someone on the board or in the C-suite, a CTO or a CEO, saw content about n8n and asked, "Why don't we do the same thing in our organization?" They bring it in and often find they're already using n8n, just in a more limited way, which makes it much easier. At some point you also want to accelerate. Partners are a great way to do that, and it works very well for us. A lot of our community consists of people who built agencies around n8n. They go out and say, "I can help you build this workflow, I can maintain it for you, I can help you figure out what can be automated." They're accelerators. A month ago we announced a partnership with Accenture, we're talking with other system integrators, and more partnerships will be announced soon. These accelerators help us reach more of our user base, because we obviously can't have a one-to-one relationship with everybody, so we use all the channels available to us. Who Should Actually Build the Automations
zh: 这是从中小企业或直接面向消费者细分起步的公司面临的共同挑战,人们构建了一个东西然后把它带进企业。除了证明你有正确的安全检查之外,入市动作看起来是什么样的?因为产品驱动增长只能带你走那么远。 Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:35:56 我们通过自下而上的增长进入了大多数组织,但有趣的是,不只是自下而上。我们也会自上而下进入,董事会或高管层的某个人,一个 CTO 或 CEO,看到了关于 n8n 的内容,然后问:「为什么我们不在自己的组织里做同样的事情?」他们把它带进来,并且常常发现他们其实已经在用 n8n 了,只是用法更有限,这让事情容易得多。到了某个时点你也会想加速。合作伙伴是做到这一点的好方式,而且这对我们非常有效。我们社区的很大一部分是围绕 n8n 建立代理商的人。他们出去说:「我可以帮你构建这个工作流,我可以为你维护它,我可以帮你想清楚哪些可以被自动化。」他们是加速器。一个月前我们宣布了与 Accenture 的合作伙伴关系,我们正在与其他系统集成商洽谈,很快还会有更多合作伙伴关系公布。这些加速器帮助我们触达更多的用户群体,因为我们显然无法与每个人保持一对一的关系,所以我们利用所有可用的渠道。到底该由谁来构建自动化

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: As you partner with consulting firms and implementation partners, one challenge, and we do this for a living too, is that you run the initial sprints, the client sees the magic and loves it, but at some point you want them to be more self-sufficient, and they want that too. So thinking about the adoption curve and maintenance: what approaches are you seeing for large enterprises? A center of excellence, a chief AI officer overseeing implementations, functional leaders handling their own automations? What's your vision? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:38:07 We see all of it out there. But success, for us and for our partners, is not just centralizing everything. If you have a centralized team building automations, assistants, or agents for other people, you get a lot of value, but you don't really empower people. You build for them, and at some point it becomes unmaintainable, because that one department has to maintain hundreds or thousands of automations. That doesn't work. It's also the opposite of why I created n8n. I built it because I saw that the people with the problems were dependent on other people, like me, to build their automations and agents. The idea behind n8n is that the people who have the problem can solve it themselves. That's why we keep making it simpler and simpler. We have an AI and automation department internally too, but its job is to empower people inside the organization, not to build everything for them. The people who have a problem should be empowered to build it themselves. The department is there if you get stuck: "I don't know how to do this one thing," and they help you, or they help you figure out what's possible in the first place. Teach people to fish. In the beginning, people have no idea what's possible, so you start small and empower them more and more. Then you document what you did and make sure the right tools are in place. The department creates the guardrails and owns education, but the building should be owned by the people who actually have the problem, because nobody can do it better than them. They know the whole process by heart. Explaining it to someone else is super inefficient, and it'll never be quite the same. For any simple change, you'd have to go back to that other person again. It's just inefficient. Measuring the ROI of AI
zh: 当你与咨询公司和实施合作伙伴合作时,一个挑战是——我们也以此为业——你跑完了最初的冲刺,客户看到了魔法并且很喜欢,但到了某个时点你想让他们更自给自足,他们自己也想。那么,关于采用曲线和维护:你在大型企业中看到了哪些做法?一个卓越中心、一个监督实施的首席 AI 官、还是职能负责人各自管理自己的自动化?你的愿景是什么? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:38:07 这些做法外面都有。但对我们和我们的合作伙伴而言,成功并不只是把一切集中化。如果你有一个集中化的团队为其他人构建自动化、助手或智能体,你能获得很多价值,但你并没有真正赋能人们。你替他们构建,而到了某个时点它会变得无法维护,因为那一个部门必须维护成百上千个自动化。那样行不通。这也与 我创建 n8n 的初衷相反。我构建它是因为我看到有问题的那些人不得不依赖其他人,比如我,来构建他们的自动化和智能体。n8n 背后的理念是,有问题的那些人可以自己解决它。这就是为什么我们不断把它做得越来越简单。我们内部也有一个 AI 与自动化部门,但它的职责是赋能组织内部的人,而不是替他们构建一切。有问题的人应该被赋能去自己构建。当你卡住时那个部门是在的:「我不知道这一件事该怎么做」,他们帮你,或者他们帮你想清楚一开始到底有哪些可能性。授人以渔。一开始,人们完全不知道什么是可能的,所以你从小处着手,越来越赋能他们。然后你把你做的记录下来,并确保合适的工具就位。那个部门创建护栏并负责教育,但构建应该由真正有问题的人来负责,因为没有人能比他们做得更好。他们对整个流程烂熟于心。把它解释给另一个人是超级低效的,而且结果永远不会完全一样。任何简单的改动,你都得再去找那个人。这就是低效。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: Exactly. And that's why this is so complicated to measure ROI on. First you need to understand what's possible, and once you taste that magic, it's hard to go back. Adoption is a good way to get started, but at some point people ask, "Where does all this productivity go?" At the same time, you can't give a one-size-fits-all answer of "here's how you measure ROI of your AI implementation." So what's your take on how the more advanced companies are taking that AI-adoption metric further? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:40:50 This is something we struggled with too, because there are so many ways to measure impact. Initially we thought the simplest thing was to track how much time it saved. But that's actually not the best measure. You can cheat very easily: an automation might run every minute and "save" ten minutes each time, but that doesn't mean it saves you crazy amounts of time. So now, internally, we care less about measuring ROI precisely, because we already know it has a lot of impact. What we want to drive forward is making sure change actually happens: that every department thinks about what they can do to drive change, how they can think differently and have more impact. Each department defines its own AI vision and sets specific things to achieve every quarter, and as a company we make sure each department reaches at least 90% of those AI targets. I don't think it's one-size-fits-all. For some, it makes sense to track time saved or money saved. You have to decide for yourself. But the most important thing right now is that certain things you can take as a given: you know it provides impact, so you just have to make sure you're applying it well. It becomes problematic when you have an unknown outcome on one side and very high spend on the other, because then it's no longer clear. That's another reason people appreciate n8n: the cost of running an AI system built with n8n is much lower, because we don't say "AI is the solution for everything." AI is one piece. You need AI, but you also want deterministic logic. For example, "approve those emails," or "do X or Y depending on a certain number," that's deterministic logic. It doesn't need an AI, because AI is expensive, less reliable, and slow. Why do it with an AI? And then you still have human-in-the-loop, which again means you can use it for business-critical use cases, not just a nice demo, because you know the AI can't do anything it's not supposed to. So the cost of running an AI system built with n8n is quite low, and the ROI is clear. In the simplest form, start by tracking time saved, then go further and track your own metrics. You can even do it dynamically: define an arbitrary metric and save that number on each execution. It might get saved as "time saved," but you can use it for whatever impact your organization is aiming for. One last thing: remember the example of the AI assistant for the online travel agency. This ROI thinking is important, but very often the value isn't just money saved. It's a better customer experience. People preferred the AI assistant because it never gets tired, it speaks any language, it works 24/7, and it has perfect context. So it's not always a single value. Some things you can drive forward without it being about saving money at all. It might be about a better customer experience. Whatever your company is striving for, that's the thing you should measure.
zh: 正是如此。而这也是为什么 ROI 这么难衡量。首先你需要理解什么是可能的,而一旦你尝到那种魔法的滋味,就很难回去了。采用是起步的好方式,但到了某个时点人们会问:「这些生产力都到哪儿去了?」与此同时,你没法给出一个放之四海皆准的答案,说「这里是你衡量 AI 实施 ROI 的方法」。那么,更先进的那些公司是如何把这个 AI 采用指标进一步推进的,你对此怎么看? Jan Oberhauser | n8n 00:40:50 这也是我们苦苦挣扎过的事情,因为衡量影响的方式太多了。最初我们以为最简单的办法是追踪节省了多少时间。但那其实并不是最好的衡量方式。你很容易作弊:一个自动化可能每分钟运行一次,每次「节省」十分钟,但这并不意味着它真的为你省下了天文数字的时间。所以现在,在内部,我们不太在意精确衡量 ROI,因为我们已经知道它有很大影响。我们想推动的是确保改变真正发生:让每个部门思考他们能做什么来推动改变,他们如何以不同方式思考并获得更大影响。每个部门定义自己的 AI 愿景,并设定每个季度要达成的具体事项,而作为一家公司,我们确保每个部门至少达成 90% 的那些 AI 目标。我不认为它是放之四海皆准的。对一些公司来说,追踪节省的时间或省下的钱是合理的。你必须自己决定。但现在最重要的事情是,某些东西你可以视为理所当然:你知道它能提供影响,所以你只要确保你把它用得好。当一边是未知的结果、另一边是非常高的支出时,问题就来了,因为那样就不再清楚了。这也是人们欣赏 n8n 的另一个原因:运行一个用 n8n 构建的 AI 系统的成本低得多,因为我们不说「AI 是一切问题的解决方案」。AI 只是一块。你需要 AI,但你也想要确定性逻辑。例如,「批准那些邮件」,或者「根据某个数字做 X 或 Y」,那是确定性逻辑。它不需要 AI,因为 AI 昂贵、可靠性更低、而且慢。为什么要用 AI 来做?然后你还有 human-in-the-loop,这又意味着你可以把它用于业务关键型用例,而不只是一个漂亮的演示,因为你知道 AI 做不了任何它不该做的事。所以运行一个用 n8n 构建的 AI 系统的成本相当低,而 ROI 是清晰的。以最简单的形式,先从追踪节省的时间开始,然后再往前走一步,追踪你自己的指标。你甚至可以动态地做:定义一个任意的指标,并在每次执行时保存那个数字。它可能被保存为「节省的时间」,但你可以把它用于你的组织所追求的任何影响。最后一件事:还记得那个在线旅游代理商的 AI 助手的例子吗。这种 ROI 思考很重要,但很多时候价值不只是省下的钱。它是更好的客户体验。人们更喜欢那个 AI 助手,因为它永不疲倦,它会说任何语言,它 7 天 24 小时工作,而且它拥有完美的上下文。所以它并不总是一个单一的价值。有些事情你可以在完全不关乎省钱的情况下推动。它可能是关于更好的客户体验。无论你的公司在追求什么,那就是你应该衡量的东西。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: I like that, because sometimes when we introduce a new tool, we feel forced to come up with ten new metrics to measure that specific tool's impact, when in reality it's all entangled and hard to isolate.
